<reason>Both sides argued crisply and stayed on the motion. PRO's core mechanism — that an unattached account keeps "cheap inventory" (rented faces, post-ban re-registration) infinitely replaceable, so verification must attach the account to a real person — was genuine, well-phrased, and forced CON to engage. But CON did the more decisive comparative work. CON isolated the motion's *distinctive* increment (government ID / deanonymization) from tools both sides accept (liveness, device and payment signals, photo-hash matching), then built the dilemma that PRO never escaped: ban-persistence requires durable retention of a document-derived identifier, which is exactly the subpoena/breach/state-demand exposure PRO promised to avoid. PRO's closing answer ("remembering doesn't mean a published citizen file") was pre-empted by CON's line that the endangered user "was never afraid of publication — he was afraid of existence." CON's Pressure Questions were the highest-value round in the debate: they extracted three usable concessions (no badge/boost/filter, so no user-visible signal; the ID catches none of the excluded user's lies; excluding him is "the price of admission"), and CON's closing crystallized exactly those. PRO answered honestly with clear A1:/A2: labels, which is creditable, but the honest answers hollowed out its own benefit side. CON's weighing (irreversible exposure for the least protected versus a delay for crews already holding fake documents) gave the clearer decision rule. CON's minor slips: calling the purchase merely "a delay" while its own fork conceded a real deterrent under retention, plus the clipped Rebuttal 2 — a real execution cost, though the lost material was a single trailing sentence. PRO under-exploited that tension and never contested the technical claim that a hashed/tokenized identifier is as exposure-generating as a stored document. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's "no third door" fork in Rebuttal 2 [B4.4–B4.5]: pointing out that PRO's "one-time attest, not a kept dossier" and "attachment makes inventory expensive after a ban" cannot both be true — you cannot ban a person you did not remember — and that retention is precisely the harm PRO promised to avoid. PRO's closing reply ("remembering isn't a published citizen file") was already anticipated and neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
